newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Insurer sees modest impact from Europe flood.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Insurer sees modest impact from Europe flood.

text.p: Floods sweeping through central Europe could cause damage of more than 10 billion marks, the world's leading reinsurer Munich Re predicted on Monday.

But estimates released by the reinsurance group, one of the most active in the affected areas of Poland, the Czech Republic and eastern Germany, indicate that insurance costs should be below previous estimates of 1.5 billion marks, with its own likely costs "relatively modest" at below 100 million marks.

"This is certainly not one of the largest incidents" ever to affect the insurance industry, Munich Re board member Wolf Otto Bauer told a news conference, noting that the flooded regions were mainly agricultural rather than industrial.
"We are also assuming that far from all the risks were covered by insurance," he said.

The floods, among the worst this century, have claimed more than 100 lives in Poland and the Czech Republic this month. Germany has escaped the worst of the floods, but damage to homes and crops has been extensive.

Preliminary calculations suggested the total economic cost of the disaster would be three to five billion marks each in Poland and the Czech Republic, and significantly lower in Germany, Munich Re (Muenchener Rueckversicherungs AG) said.
The cost to insurers would be some 10 percent of total damages in Poland and the Czech Republic, or up to 500 million marks in each country at the worst.
Munich Re last week estimated total insurance costs from the flood at 1.5 billion marks. Bauer said that figure came from broad market estimates, not its own research, and was unreliable.
At the same time, Bauer warned that much work had to be done accurately to assess the full impact of the flood damage.
"Clearly the waters have to recede. The primary insurers also need to carry out investigations which could take several weeks," Bauer said.
Metereological experts at Munich Re described the flooding, which has pushed water levels on the east German Oder river to the highest levels this century, as "highly unusual".
"In general, Europe is moving toward drier summers in the medium term. But it is consistent with this to have extremes from time to time," said Gerhard Berz, head of a Munich Re research division.
Officials praised the quality of the dikes in all the affected areas, which they said had held out far longer than might have been expected.
Bauer declined to estimate the cost of the flooding in Germany where thousands are preparing for evacuation from the Oderbruch area.

Large sections of the dike in Oderbruch have collapsed during the past few days, but thousands of German soldiers, aid workers and local residents have worked round-the-clock shifts for days to prevent a breach.

Munich Re itself expected to pay out "tens of millions" of marks related to the whole central European region, with the figure at risk of passing 100 million marks only if the situation became radically worse.
Allianz AG, the German market leader in primary insurance, said last week it expected significant claims from water damage in the eastern states.
The company acquired some 3.4 million home insurance policies and a further 1.1 million building policies when it took over the state insurer for the former Communist-controlled region in 1990.
Munich Re said some two thirds of private households in eastern Germany were insured for flood damage, which formed part of standard contracts until 1990.
In Poland, regular household insurance had flood cover as standard whereas only about half of Czech households had paid the additional premium needed there for flood protection.
